# Essay guidance for the reader's notes

**DRAFT for the owner's review.** Written 2026-10-28 from 54 sources (34 on the craft, 20 on the approach) in
[sources.json](sources.json). Nothing here runs until the owner has read, edited, and merged it.

This is what the reader (the reviewer in `specs/product/essays/reviewer.md`) knows about college essays before it
reads a draft. Each section below is loaded by its heading: the eight categories of note first, then the five
questions of approach. Every paragraph says where its advice comes from. Where the sources disagree, the paragraph says
so, and the reader asks the student a question instead of taking a side. The reader is writing notes for a
seventeen-year-old: it names what it noticed and why a reader of applications would care, and it never writes a
sentence for the essay. The last section lists the questions the owner should settle before the reviewer runs.

## mechanics

A run-on and a comma splice are the same mistake made two ways: two complete sentences joined with no punctuation, or
with only a comma. Writing centers agree on the fixes: a period, a semicolon, or a comma with *and*, *but*, *or*, *so*,
*for*, *nor*, or *yet* ([UNC Writing Center](https://writingcenter.unc.edu/tips-and-tools/fragments-and-run-ons/);
[Purdue OWL](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/general_writing/punctuation/independent_and_dependent_clauses/runonsentences.html);
[Utah Valley University Writing Center](https://www.uvu.edu/writingcenter/handouts/comma-splices.html)). A run-on
need not be long, and a sentence with *and* but no comma before it can still be one
([Wake Forest Writing Center](https://prod.wp.cdn.aws.wfu.edu/sites/579/2026/08/Run-Ons-and-Comma-Splices.pdf)). A
fragment is the reverse: a clause that starts with *because*, *when*, or *although* and never finishes its thought
([UNC Writing Center](https://writingcenter.unc.edu/tips-and-tools/fragments-and-run-ons/)).

Spell checkers miss a wrong word that is still a word (*their* for *there*, *to* for *too*), and pasting into an
application's text box can change punctuation, so the last read should happen in the form itself
([UNC Writing Center](https://writingcenter.unc.edu/tips-and-tools/editing-and-proofreading/);
[Georgia Tech Admission](https://admission.gatech.edu/first-year/personal-essays)). Getting the college's own name
wrong is the error admissions readers mention most by name: it does not sink an application, but it plants a doubt about
interest ([Georgia Tech Admission blog](https://sites.gatech.edu/admission-blog/2019/07/12/will-saying-im-a-blueberry-get-me-into-college-supplemental-essays-101)).
Over the limit is a mechanics problem too: MIT's form will not save a response that runs long, and writing centers say
to follow word limits exactly ([MIT Admissions](https://mitadmissions.org/help/faq/essays-word-count/);
[UNC Writing Center](https://writingcenter.unc.edu/tips-and-tools/application-essays/)).

Small, fixable things a reader can point at: a sentence that buries its subject behind a long interruption, a passive
sentence where the actor matters, a string of negatives, a redundant pair such as *each and every*
([Purdue OWL](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/general_writing/mechanics/sentence_clarity.html);
[UW–Madison Writing Center](https://writing.wisc.edu/handbook/grammarandstyle/ccs_activevoice/);
[UNC Writing Center](https://writingcenter.unc.edu/tips-and-tools/conciseness-handout/)). These are style choices more
than errors, and the passive voice has good uses, so the reader marks them only when the sentence is hard to follow.

**Where sources disagree: how much errors count.** The University of California says plainly that it does not grade
grammar or spelling in its personal insight questions, though errors distract; MIT says its essays are not a writing
test; the Coalition's revision guide says not to obsess over any one word
([University of California](https://admission.universityofcalifornia.edu/how-to-apply/applying-as-a-first-year/personal-insight-questions.html);
[MIT Admissions](https://mitadmissions.org/apply/firstyear/essays-activities-academics/);
[Coalition for College](https://www.coalitionforcollegeaccess.org/mycoalition-counselor-all/revising-college-essays-t3dkj)).
Vanderbilt and NYU treat a clean, polished page as part of what the application shows
([Vanderbilt Admissions](https://admissions.vanderbilt.edu/vandybloggers/2013/09/how-to-write-your-personal-essay/);
[NYU Admissions](https://meet.nyu.edu/advice/tips-for-writing-a-winning-activities-section/)). So the reader marks
every real error (that is what `mechanics` notes are for, and the only notes that carry a `fix`), but its `why` says an
error distracts a reader, never that it costs admission. Where a break from the rules may be deliberate (a fragment
for effect, a one-line paragraph), the reader asks whether it was meant rather than correcting it.

Order of work matters: writing centers advise fixing ideas first and proofreading last, because polishing early makes
a draft feel finished before it is ([Purdue OWL](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/general_writing/undergraduate_applications/undergraduate_application_timeline/advice_for_writing_application_essays.html);
[UNC Writing Center](https://writingcenter.unc.edu/tips-and-tools/editing-and-proofreading/)). On an early draft the
reader keeps mechanics notes few and says the rest can wait.

## prompt

The first test of any essay is whether it answers the question that was asked. Admissions offices and writing centers
say this more than anything else, often with an apology for saying something so obvious
([Coalition for College, from Johns Hopkins](https://www.coalitionforcollegeaccess.org/mycoalition-counselor-all/pro-tips-on-writing-your-personal-statement);
[UNC Writing Center](https://writingcenter.unc.edu/tips-and-tools/application-essays/);
[Georgia Tech Admission](https://admission.gatech.edu/first-year/personal-essays)). Johns Hopkins walks students
through its own prompt part by part and asks them to answer each part
([Johns Hopkins Admissions](https://apply.jhu.edu/hopkins-insider/advice-for-crafting-your-supplemental-essay/)). A
prompt with two questions ("what have you learned, and how has it shaped you") gets a note when the draft answers only
one.

A prompt is a frame, not a cage. Broad prompts are broad on purpose; UVA's dean calls the topic a vehicle, and the UC
says all of its questions get equal consideration, with no advantage to any one
([University of Virginia](https://as.virginia.edu/news/uva-admission-essays-are-posted-learn-how-write-your-best-one);
[University of California](https://admission.universityofcalifornia.edu/how-to-apply/applying-as-a-first-year/personal-insight-questions.html);
[Tufts Admissions](https://admissions.tufts.edu/blogs/inside-admissions/post/essay-writing-tips/)). So the reader
does not question the choice of prompt or topic; it asks whether the draft, as written, gets to what the prompt asks.

A draft written for one prompt and reused for another often answers the first one. Writing centers warn against one
statement for every application and against boilerplate across colleges whose prompts differ slightly
([Purdue OWL](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/job_search_writing/preparing_an_application/writing_the_personal_statement/index.html);
[Purdue OWL](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/general_writing/undergraduate_applications/undergraduate_application_timeline/advice_for_writing_application_essays.html)).
When a draft is linked to several prompts, the reader reads it against the prompt it is being reviewed for and notes
the sentence where it drifts.

A "why us" that could be sent to any college does not answer its prompt, and naming the wrong college certainly does
not; both are `prompt` notes as well as `interest` notes (see [interest](#interest))
([Coalition for College](https://www.coalitionforcollegeaccess.org/mycoalition-counselor-all/answering-why-this-college-essay-questions);
[Georgia Tech Admission blog](https://sites.gatech.edu/admission-blog/2019/07/12/will-saying-im-a-blueberry-get-me-into-college-supplemental-essays-101)).

## specific

The most repeated piece of craft advice is to show rather than tell: a claim about yourself (resourceful, a leader,
curious) needs a moment that shows it, or the reader has no reason to believe it
([Purdue OWL](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/general_writing/undergraduate_applications/undergraduate_application_timeline/documents/admissions_essay_handout.pdf);
[Purdue OWL](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/job_search_writing/preparing_an_application/writing_the_personal_statement/index.html);
[University of California](https://admission.universityofcalifornia.edu/how-to-apply/applying-as-a-first-year/personal-insight-questions.html)).
Purdue's application-essay page asks for evidence that answers how and why, not only what
([Purdue OWL](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/general_writing/undergraduate_applications/undergraduate_application_timeline/advice_for_writing_application_essays.html)).

UNC's writing center gives a test a reader can use: cut anything that could be pasted into anyone else's application,
and look for the good, specific sentence that often comes right after a general one
([UNC Writing Center](https://writingcenter.unc.edu/tips-and-tools/application-essays/)). Platitudes ("I'm a people
person") are the usual sign. A `specific` note points at the general sentence and asks what happened, when, with
whom; if the next sentence already does the work, the note says so.

Detail is how an essay stops sounding like everyone's. Tufts describes the choice as going broad (a list of things
you like) or going deep (one thing, closely), and says deep is better
([Tufts Admissions](https://admissions.tufts.edu/blogs/inside-admissions/post/the-only-four-college-essay-writing-tips-youll-ever-need/)).
The moment does not need to be dramatic: Johns Hopkins says small, one-time moments can carry an essay, and Purdue
says a successful essay does not need a life-changing event
([Johns Hopkins Admissions](https://apply.jhu.edu/hopkins-insider/advice-for-crafting-your-supplemental-essay/);
[Purdue OWL](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/general_writing/undergraduate_applications/undergraduate_application_timeline/advice_for_writing_application_essays.html)).
The reader never suggests a bigger story.

## structure

Many weak openings start too early or too generally: the sweeping statement about all of history, the dictionary
definition, the paragraph that restates the question ([UNC Writing Center](https://writingcenter.unc.edu/tips-and-tools/introductions/)).
The opening paragraph matters most for a reader who reads quickly, and handouts on application essays say to make it
count ([Purdue OWL](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/job_search_writing/preparing_an_application/writing_the_personal_statement/index.html);
[Purdue OWL](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/general_writing/undergraduate_applications/undergraduate_application_timeline/documents/admissions_essay_handout.pdf)).
A common `structure` note: the essay seems to begin in its second or third paragraph; what would it lose if it began
there? UNC also suggests writing the introduction last, which is a fair thing to mention on an early draft
([UNC Writing Center](https://writingcenter.unc.edu/tips-and-tools/introductions/)).

Endings that only restate what came before add nothing; writing centers ask a conclusion to say why the story matters
(the "so what?" test) ([UNC Writing Center](https://writingcenter.unc.edu/tips-and-tools/conclusions/);
[Purdue OWL](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/general_writing/undergraduate_applications/undergraduate_application_timeline/documents/admissions_essay_handout.pdf)).
A paragraph should do one job; a paragraph that changes subject halfway is a fair note
([UNC Writing Center](https://writingcenter.unc.edu/tips-and-tools/paragraphs/)). The whole essay should be about one
thing, and a friend should be able to say in a sentence what its point is
([Purdue OWL](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/general_writing/undergraduate_applications/undergraduate_application_timeline/advice_for_writing_application_essays.html);
[Coalition for College](https://www.coalitionforcollegeaccess.org/mycoalition-counselor-all/revising-college-essays-t3dkj)).

A college essay is not a school essay. NACAC says the personal statement needs no thesis and no five-paragraph frame,
and UVA's dean tells students not to feel bound by the formula they learned for class
([NACAC](https://www.nacacnet.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/NACAC-GCAP-2022-Report-1022_1.pdf);
[University of Virginia](https://as.virginia.edu/news/uva-admission-essays-are-posted-learn-how-write-your-best-one)).
So the reader never asks for a thesis statement or a topic sentence, and never treats an unusual shape as a flaw. It
notes structure only when the shape gets in the way of the point.

## voice

Admissions offices want the essay to sound like the student. Yale says an essay that doesn't sound like its writer
cannot work as a personal statement; Tufts asks students to write the way they speak
([Yale Admissions](https://admissions.yale.edu/what-yale-looks-for);
[Tufts Admissions](https://admissions.tufts.edu/blogs/inside-admissions/post/the-only-four-college-essay-writing-tips-youll-ever-need/);
[Princeton Admission](https://admission.princeton.edu/apply/before-you-apply/helpful-tips)). Writing centers warn
against the thesaurus, against trying to sound intelligent, and against words a student would not use
([UNC Writing Center](https://writingcenter.unc.edu/tips-and-tools/word-choice/);
[UNC Writing Center](https://writingcenter.unc.edu/tips-and-tools/style/)). A `voice` note points at the phrase that
sounds borrowed (a brochure, a résumé, a thesaurus) and asks how the student would say it out loud.

Readers notice when an adult wrote the essay. Vanderbilt observes that a parent's prose reads differently from a
student's, and the Coalition warns that heavy editing, by people or by AI tools, can sand a voice flat
([Vanderbilt Admissions](https://admissions.vanderbilt.edu/vandybloggers/2013/09/how-to-write-your-personal-essay/);
[Coalition for College](https://www.coalitionforcollegeaccess.org/mycoalition-counselor-all/revising-college-essays-t3dkj);
[Coalition for College](https://www.coalitionforcollegeaccess.org/mycoalition-counselor-all/ai-and-the-college-essay)).
Princeton and the UC require that the essay be the student's own work
([Princeton Admission](https://admission.princeton.edu/apply/before-you-apply/helpful-tips);
[University of California](https://admission.universityofcalifornia.edu/how-to-apply/applying-as-a-first-year/personal-insight-questions.html)).
This is the deepest reason the reader never rewrites: a note that offered better sentences would do exactly what these
offices warn against. The reader also does not guess whether a draft was written by a model; it notes only what reads
like an adult or a brochure.

A list of accomplishments is a voice problem as well as a showcase problem: it reads like the activities section, not
like a person ([Vanderbilt Admissions](https://admissions.vanderbilt.edu/vandybloggers/2013/09/how-to-write-your-personal-essay/);
[University of California](https://admission.universityofcalifornia.edu/how-to-apply/applying-as-a-first-year/personal-insight-questions.html)).
Drama works the same way in reverse: UNC warns against invented drama and melodrama
([UNC Writing Center](https://writingcenter.unc.edu/tips-and-tools/application-essays/)).

**Where sources disagree: humor and risk.** Purdue's handout lists gimmicks, clichés, and humor as risks; Vanderbilt
says feel free to be funny but don't overreach; Tufts says a natural joker can write a funny essay
([Purdue OWL](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/general_writing/undergraduate_applications/undergraduate_application_timeline/documents/admissions_essay_handout.pdf);
[Vanderbilt Admissions](https://admissions.vanderbilt.edu/vandybloggers/2013/09/how-to-write-your-personal-essay/);
[Tufts Admissions](https://admissions.tufts.edu/blogs/inside-admissions/post/essay-writing-tips/)). The reader does not
tell a student to add or remove humor. When a joke may not land, it asks whether the joke sounds like the student and
what it shows.

**Where sources disagree: how many readers.** Tufts and the Coalition say show the essay to two people and stop; Yale
says at least one or two; UVA's dean says it would be foolish to submit without someone you trust reading it, but that
it should not read as if a committee wrote it
([Tufts Admissions](https://admissions.tufts.edu/blogs/inside-admissions/post/the-only-four-college-essay-writing-tips-youll-ever-need/);
[Coalition for College](https://www.coalitionforcollegeaccess.org/mycoalition-counselor-all/revising-college-essays-t3dkj);
[Yale Admissions](https://admissions.yale.edu/essays);
[University of Virginia](https://as.virginia.edu/news/uva-admission-essays-are-posted-learn-how-write-your-best-one)).
They agree on the risk (too many editors) more than on the number. Quad's reader is one more reader, so it keeps its
notes few, and it never asks the student to take a parent's or counselor's comment.

**Where sources disagree: AI tools.** The Coalition's guidance allows AI for brainstorming, outlining, and checking
grammar, as long as the ideas and stories are the student's; it also says some colleges have their own AI policies,
and Bowdoin publishes one ([Coalition for College](https://www.coalitionforcollegeaccess.org/mycoalition-counselor-all/ai-and-the-college-essay);
[Bowdoin Admissions](https://www.bowdoin.edu/admissions/apply/index.html)). Quad's reader is itself an AI tool that
gives notes, not text. Until the owner decides whether it should remind students to check each college's AI policy
(see the end of this file), the reader gives no advice on tools; if a draft raises the subject, it asks whether the
student has read that college's policy.

## care

Some subjects are the student's to share or not. Vanderbilt's admissions staff tell students they don't have to include
anything they aren't comfortable sharing, and UNC's writing center warns about subjects that may put a reader off
([Vanderbilt Admissions](https://admissions.vanderbilt.edu/vandybloggers/2013/09/how-to-write-your-personal-essay/);
[UNC Writing Center](https://writingcenter.unc.edu/tips-and-tools/application-essays/)). Other sources invite exactly
these subjects: the UC's questions ask about barriers students have faced, and Purdue's personal statement guide lists
personal and family problems among the details that can help a committee understand an applicant
([University of California](https://admission.universityofcalifornia.edu/how-to-apply/applying-as-a-first-year/personal-insight-questions.html);
[Purdue OWL](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/job_search_writing/preparing_an_application/writing_the_personal_statement/index.html)).
The sources disagree on how personal is too personal, so a `care` note is always a question, never an instruction: it
names what the draft discloses and asks whether the student means to share it and whether the essay needs it.

Another person's story is a different matter. A draft that names a sibling's diagnosis, a friend's crisis, or a
parent's job loss tells someone else's story; Purdue's handout and Tufts both remind students to keep the focus on
themselves, with others as "guest stars" or launching pads
([Purdue OWL](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/general_writing/undergraduate_applications/undergraduate_application_timeline/documents/admissions_essay_handout.pdf);
[Tufts Admissions](https://admissions.tufts.edu/blogs/inside-admissions/post/the-only-four-college-essay-writing-tips-youll-ever-need/)).
A `care` note may ask whether that person would be comfortable with it, and what the detail does for the essay.

Hard circumstances have other places to go. The Common App's Responsibilities and Circumstances and Additional
Information sections, and the UC's additional comments field, exist for context that doesn't belong in an essay
([Georgia Tech Admission](https://admission.gatech.edu/first-year/personal-essays);
[University of California](https://admission.universityofcalifornia.edu/how-to-apply/applying-as-a-first-year/personal-insight-questions.html)).
A reader may mention that these exist; it never tells a student to move or remove a subject.

Georgia Tech states that its admission staff are mandatory reporters who must report suspected abuse or neglect of a
minor described anywhere in an application ([Georgia Tech Admission](https://admission.gatech.edu/first-year/personal-essays)).
Other colleges may be bound by similar rules. The reader is not a counselor and does not advise on disclosure; when a
draft describes harm to the student, the note is a question with no advice in it, and the owner should decide what
else Quad shows (see the end of this file).

Honesty is part of care. Writers should not invent drama or stories, and the Coalition's AI guidance says no tool should
create experiences the student didn't have ([UNC Writing Center](https://writingcenter.unc.edu/tips-and-tools/application-essays/);
[Coalition for College](https://www.coalitionforcollegeaccess.org/mycoalition-counselor-all/ai-and-the-college-essay)).
The reader never suggests a detail the student hasn't written.

## showcase

The essay's job is to show what the rest of the application doesn't. NACAC calls this the essay's primary purpose;
the Coalition's tips from Johns Hopkins say to tell the reader something new rather than list activities again; Georgia
Tech's reader puts it as "tell me something I might not already know about you"
([NACAC](https://www.nacacnet.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/NACAC-GCAP-2022-Report-1022_1.pdf);
[Coalition for College, from Johns Hopkins](https://www.coalitionforcollegeaccess.org/mycoalition-counselor-all/pro-tips-on-writing-your-personal-statement);
[Georgia Tech Admission blog](https://sites.gatech.edu/admission-blog/2026/10/06/coffee-conversations-and-completing-your-college-application/)).
Vanderbilt, the UC, and Purdue's handout say the same about summarizing activities and achievements the readers
already have ([Vanderbilt Admissions](https://admissions.vanderbilt.edu/vandybloggers/2013/09/how-to-write-your-personal-essay/);
[University of California](https://admission.universityofcalifornia.edu/how-to-apply/applying-as-a-first-year/personal-insight-questions.html);
[Purdue OWL](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/general_writing/undergraduate_applications/undergraduate_application_timeline/documents/admissions_essay_handout.pdf)).

So a `showcase` note compares the draft with what the reader knows about the record (the story, the depth reading,
the other drafts' first lines), since an essay works together with the rest of the application and does not stand
alone, and each essay for a college should show a different part of the student
([Coalition for College, from Johns Hopkins](https://www.coalitionforcollegeaccess.org/mycoalition-counselor-all/pro-tips-on-writing-your-personal-statement);
[Tufts Admissions](https://admissions.tufts.edu/blogs/inside-admissions/post/application-checklist-the-supplement)).
It notes an essay that repeats the activities list, an essay that never reaches what the record says the student went
deepest in, and several essays for one college that all show the same trait. It asks; it does not choose the topic.

The topic matters less than what the student does with it. Yale has read wonderful essays on common topics and weak
ones on unusual topics, and says the writer's perspective matters more than the subject
([Yale Admissions](https://admissions.yale.edu/essays)). The Coalition's member colleges say there is no particular
story they are looking for ([Coalition for College](https://www.coalitionforcollegeaccess.org/mycoalition-counselor-all/getting-started-on-your-college-essay)).
This is why the rubric forbids calling a topic "overdone": the sources say a common topic is fine when the essay is
the student's own.

Students often write about someone or something else: a grandparent, a team, a trip. Tufts and Vanderbilt both say
those can be the way in, but the essay has to come back to the student
([Tufts Admissions](https://admissions.tufts.edu/blogs/inside-admissions/post/the-only-four-college-essay-writing-tips-youll-ever-need/);
[Vanderbilt Admissions](https://admissions.vanderbilt.edu/vandybloggers/2013/09/how-to-write-your-personal-essay/)).
A note can ask where the student is in a paragraph that is all about someone else.

## interest

A "why us" essay is about the student and the college together. The Coalition says admissions counselors want
thoughtful, specific reasons and clear connections between the student and the college, not praise; NACAC says to
leave out the general draws (size, location, weather, reputation) that every applicant shares
([Coalition for College](https://www.coalitionforcollegeaccess.org/mycoalition-counselor-all/answering-why-this-college-essay-questions);
[NACAC](https://www.nacacnet.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/NACAC-GCAP-2022-Report-1022_1.pdf)).

The test that admissions offices give is simple: replace the college's name with another's, and if the essay still
works, it is not specific enough ([Tufts Admissions](https://admissions.tufts.edu/blogs/inside-admissions/post/essay-advice-the-ghost-of-my-supplement-past/);
[Coalition for College](https://www.coalitionforcollegeaccess.org/mycoalition-counselor-all/answering-why-this-college-essay-questions)).
Lines lifted from the college's "about" page fail the same test; Georgia Tech says a reader recognizes them at once
([Georgia Tech Admission blog](https://sites.gatech.edu/admission-blog/2019/07/12/will-saying-im-a-blueberry-get-me-into-college-supplemental-essays-101)).
The reader has the college's facts from the site (programs, size, setting) so it can tell a specific claim from a
brochure line; a note names the line that fits any college and asks what the student found there that they could not
find elsewhere.

Specific means a program, a course, a research group, a club, a tradition, or a way of learning the college describes,
tied to something the student has done or wants to do ([Tufts Admissions](https://admissions.tufts.edu/blogs/inside-admissions/post/application-checklist-the-supplement);
[Johns Hopkins Admissions](https://apply.jhu.edu/hopkins-insider/application-resources-and-suggestions/);
[UW–Madison Writing Center](https://writing.wisc.edu/handbook/professionalwriting/writing-personal-statements-for-academic-programs/)).
Naming things is not enough: the Coalition lists "facts without explaining why they matter" among the common
weaknesses, and says a few examples explained beat everything the college offers listed
([Coalition for College](https://www.coalitionforcollegeaccess.org/mycoalition-counselor-all/answering-why-this-college-essay-questions)).
An `interest` note may ask why a named program matters to this student.

Princeton and Rice frame their questions as what the student would do there, not only why they like it
([Princeton Admission](https://admission.princeton.edu/apply/before-you-apply/helpful-tips);
[Rice Admission](https://admission.rice.edu/apply/first-year-domestic-applicants)). A draft that describes only the
past, when the prompt asks about the future at that college, gets a `prompt` or `interest` note.

## approach: what to showcase

Colleges that read holistically say they read the whole person: academics first, then how a student spends their time,
then personal qualities, with essays and recommendations carrying the last of these
([Coalition for College, from Harvard](https://www.coalitionforcollegeaccess.org/mycoalition-counselor-all/harvard-what-colleges-are-looking-for);
[Yale Admissions](https://admissions.yale.edu/what-yale-looks-for)). MIT says the match between the student and the
place drives its decisions, more than the numbers do ([MIT Admissions](https://mitadmissions.org/apply/process/what-we-look-for/)).
So the reader treats the essays as the place where a file's personal side comes through: what the student cares
about, how they think, how they treat other people.

Choosing what to show starts from the student, not the reader. Georgia Tech's admission blog asks students to stop
asking "what do they want" and ask "why do I do what I do"; MIT, Vanderbilt, and Georgia Tech's essay page all warn
against guessing what admissions officers want to hear
([Georgia Tech Admission blog](https://sites.gatech.edu/admission-blog/2024/10/07/preparing-your-college-application-you-are-asking-the-wrong-questions/);
[MIT Admissions](https://mitadmissions.org/apply/firstyear/essays-activities-academics/);
[Vanderbilt Admissions](https://admissions.vanderbilt.edu/vandybloggers/2013/09/how-to-write-your-personal-essay/);
[Georgia Tech Admission](https://admission.gatech.edu/first-year/personal-essays)). When a draft seems written to
impress, the reader asks what the student wanted a reader to know about them.

The essay should add to the file, not repeat it, and should be about one thing rather than everything
([NACAC](https://www.nacacnet.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/NACAC-GCAP-2022-Report-1022_1.pdf);
[Purdue OWL](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/general_writing/undergraduate_applications/undergraduate_application_timeline/documents/admissions_essay_handout.pdf)).
NACAC says the personal statement should not be a narrative résumé
([NACAC](https://www.nacacnet.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/NACAC-GCAP-2022-Report-1022_1.pdf)).

## approach: the main essay and the supplements

The main essay goes to every college, so it should not be tailored to one; the supplements are where each college asks
its own questions ([NACAC](https://www.nacacnet.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/NACAC-GCAP-2022-Report-1022_1.pdf);
[Johns Hopkins Admissions](https://apply.jhu.edu/hopkins-insider/advice-for-crafting-your-supplemental-essay/)).
Supplements are short, but NACAC, Georgia Tech, and the Coalition all say they are read closely and deserve the same
care as the main essay ([NACAC](https://www.nacacnet.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/NACAC-GCAP-2022-Report-1022_1.pdf);
[Georgia Tech Admission blog](https://sites.gatech.edu/admission-blog/2019/07/12/will-saying-im-a-blueberry-get-me-into-college-supplemental-essays-101);
[Coalition for College](https://www.coalitionforcollegeaccess.org/mycoalition-counselor-all/standout-supplemental-essays)).
A rushed supplement written at the end of the process is the case Georgia Tech describes; the reader treats a
supplement's draft with the same attention as the main essay's.

The pieces should divide the work. Tufts advises that each essay touch a different part of who the student is, and
Georgia Tech asks students to use a supplement for what they have not had a chance to say
([Tufts Admissions](https://admissions.tufts.edu/blogs/inside-admissions/post/application-checklist-the-supplement);
[Georgia Tech Admission blog](https://sites.gatech.edu/admission-blog/2019/07/12/will-saying-im-a-blueberry-get-me-into-college-supplemental-essays-101)).
The reader sees the first lines of the student's other drafts for the same college, so a `showcase` note can say "the
main essay already covers this" and ask what this one could add.

**Where sources disagree: reusing a draft.** Purdue says not to use one essay everywhere but allows adapting an essay for
similar prompts; UT Austin accepts an essay the student has already written for another prompt; NACAC says a "why us"
should be so specific to one college that it cannot be recycled
([Purdue OWL](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/general_writing/undergraduate_applications/undergraduate_application_timeline/advice_for_writing_application_essays.html);
[UT Austin Admissions](https://admissions.utexas.edu/apply/application-materials/essays-and-short-answers/);
[NACAC](https://www.nacacnet.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/NACAC-GCAP-2022-Report-1022_1.pdf)). The reader does not
object to reuse, which the workspace supports. It reads a reused draft against the prompt at hand and asks about the
sentences that belong to another college or another question.

**Where sources disagree: optional essays.** NACAC says an optional essay is rarely truly optional, since skipping it
can read as low interest; the Coalition says students are not expected to do everything and that demonstrated interest
is rarely decisive on its own ([NACAC](https://www.nacacnet.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/NACAC-GCAP-2022-Report-1022_1.pdf);
[Coalition for College](https://www.coalitionforcollegeaccess.org/mycoalition-counselor-all/demonstrated-interest-what-it-means-and-why-it-matters)).
The reader reviews the drafts it is given and never tells a student to write, or skip, an optional essay; a draft for
an optional prompt is read like any other, and if the student asks whether it matters, the reader points them to the
college's own words rather than answering.

## approach: depth

Admissions offices prefer a few things done with care to many things listed. MIT says it doesn't expect applicants to
do a million things and asks them to put their heart into a few; NYU asks students to rank activities by what matters
most to them, not by what looks impressive ([MIT Admissions](https://mitadmissions.org/apply/process/what-we-look-for/);
[NYU Admissions](https://meet.nyu.edu/advice/tips-for-writing-a-winning-activities-section/)). Harvard, writing for
the Coalition, says the way a student has spent their time, told in the activities section or the essays, shows what
has mattered to them ([Coalition for College, from Harvard](https://www.coalitionforcollegeaccess.org/mycoalition-counselor-all/harvard-what-colleges-are-looking-for)).

An essay feeds that depth by going inside one thread rather than across many. Tufts's "go deep" advice, Purdue's
warning that covering too much makes every part shallow, and UW–Madison's advice to focus on two or three
representative experiences all point the same way
([Tufts Admissions](https://admissions.tufts.edu/blogs/inside-admissions/post/the-only-four-college-essay-writing-tips-youll-ever-need/);
[Purdue OWL](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/general_writing/undergraduate_applications/undergraduate_application_timeline/documents/admissions_essay_handout.pdf);
[UW–Madison Writing Center](https://writing.wisc.edu/handbook/professionalwriting/writing-personal-statements-for-academic-programs/)).
Georgia Tech asks students to explain why they do an activity, not only what they did
([Georgia Tech Admission blog](https://sites.gatech.edu/admission-blog/2024/10/07/preparing-your-college-application-you-are-asking-the-wrong-questions/)).

The reader knows the three or four things the record says the student has gone deepest in. When the essay mentions one
in passing, or lists it, a `showcase` note can ask whether a moment from it would do more than the list does
([Tufts Admissions](https://admissions.tufts.edu/blogs/inside-admissions/post/the-only-four-college-essay-writing-tips-youll-ever-need/)).
When the essay is about something else entirely, that is the student's choice, and the reader says nothing about depth
unless the prompt asks about an activity or a major; MIT, for one, says it is not particular about which things a
student cares about ([MIT Admissions](https://mitadmissions.org/apply/process/what-we-look-for/)).

## approach: showing interest

Demonstrated interest is how a student engages with a college: visits, events, emails, interviews, the round they
apply in. Colleges differ, some don't track it, and it is rarely decisive on its own
([Coalition for College](https://www.coalitionforcollegeaccess.org/mycoalition-counselor-all/demonstrated-interest-what-it-means-and-why-it-matters);
[NACAC](https://www.nacacnet.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/NACAC-GCAP-2022-Report-1022_1.pdf)). For colleges that
do track it, NACAC says the care in a "why us" essay is itself one of the signals
([NACAC](https://www.nacacnet.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/NACAC-GCAP-2022-Report-1022_1.pdf)).

Interest in an essay comes from research the student actually did. Georgia Tech says real research starts with
curiosity; Johns Hopkins's student contributor suggests the club list, the course catalog, the research listings, and
anything that stood out on a visit; Tufts asks students to name a program, project, or club they want to join
([Georgia Tech Admission blog](https://sites.gatech.edu/admission-blog/2019/07/12/will-saying-im-a-blueberry-get-me-into-college-supplemental-essays-101);
[Johns Hopkins Admissions](https://apply.jhu.edu/hopkins-insider/application-resources-and-suggestions/);
[Tufts Admissions](https://admissions.tufts.edu/blogs/inside-admissions/post/application-checklist-the-supplement)).
The reader can see the interest acts the student logged (a visit, an interview); when the draft could use what the
student saw there, the note asks about it. It never asks the student to claim a visit or a contact they didn't log.

The connection runs both ways: why this college fits the student, and what the student would do there
([Coalition for College](https://www.coalitionforcollegeaccess.org/mycoalition-counselor-all/answering-why-this-college-essay-questions);
[Princeton Admission](https://admission.princeton.edu/apply/before-you-apply/helpful-tips)). A draft that lists the
college's strengths without the student in them gets an `interest` note asking where the student fits.

## approach: short answers

Short answers are short on purpose: MIT asks for 40 to 50 words on some questions, Yale for 200 characters, UT Austin
for about one paragraph ([MIT Admissions](https://mitadmissions.org/apply/firstyear/essays-activities-academics/);
[Yale Admissions](https://admissions.yale.edu/essays);
[UT Austin Admissions](https://admissions.utexas.edu/apply/application-materials/essays-and-short-answers/)). At that
length, UNC's writing center says, the answer needs more detail and less preamble: get straight to the point and
answer what was asked ([UNC Writing Center](https://writingcenter.unc.edu/tips-and-tools/application-essays/)).

A short answer is not a small essay. It does not need an opening, a turn, and a conclusion; it needs a direct answer
and one telling detail. Georgia Tech says even an odd question ("what fruit are you?") deserves a real answer, because
its purpose is to show how the student thinks
([Georgia Tech Admission blog](https://sites.gatech.edu/admission-blog/2019/07/12/will-saying-im-a-blueberry-get-me-into-college-supplemental-essays-101)).
A `structure` note on a short answer is usually that it spends half its words getting started.

The activities list works the same way: NYU says each description should read like a well-composed tweet, with clear
roles and no unexplained acronyms, and that errors there stand out next to a polished essay
([NYU Admissions](https://meet.nyu.edu/advice/tips-for-writing-a-winning-activities-section/)). The reader does not
review the activities list today, but a short answer that repeats it gets the same `showcase` note as an essay would.

## Questions for the owner

1. **AI policies.** Some colleges publish their own rules on AI in applications (the Coalition and Bowdoin point to
   them). Should the reader's notes, or the editor, remind students to check each college's policy, given that the
   reader is itself an AI tool? ([Coalition for College](https://www.coalitionforcollegeaccess.org/mycoalition-counselor-all/ai-and-the-college-essay))
2. **Harm and mandatory reporting.** When a draft describes abuse or neglect, should Quad show anything beyond the
   reader's question, such as a line that admission staff at many colleges must report what they read, or a pointer to
   a counselor? ([Georgia Tech Admission](https://admission.gatech.edu/first-year/personal-essays))
3. **How hard to press on mechanics.** The sources split on how much errors count (the UC doesn't grade them; Vanderbilt
   and NYU treat polish as part of the work). This draft marks every error but explains it as a distraction, not a cost.
   Is that the right tone? ([University of California](https://admission.universityofcalifornia.edu/how-to-apply/applying-as-a-first-year/personal-insight-questions.html))
4. **Optional essays.** NACAC says optional is rarely optional; the Coalition says interest is rarely decisive. This
   draft stays out of it. Should the plan, rather than the reader, say anything?
   ([NACAC](https://www.nacacnet.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/NACAC-GCAP-2022-Report-1022_1.pdf))
5. **Older pages.** Vanderbilt's tips date from 2013, Georgia Tech's supplemental-essay post from 2019, UVA's dean's
   tips from 2018; their advice matches newer pages, but should the corpus keep sources more than five years old?
   ([Vanderbilt Admissions](https://admissions.vanderbilt.edu/vandybloggers/2013/09/how-to-write-your-personal-essay/))
6. **Missing voices.** Nothing here comes from the Common App directly: its terms allow linking only to its homepage,
   and its essay pages render only in a browser, so Georgia Tech's page on the Common App essay stands in for it
   ([Georgia Tech Admission](https://admission.gatech.edu/first-year/personal-essays)). The Harvard College Writing
   Center and Michigan's admissions site refused the crawler, UChicago's essay page renders only in a browser, and
   UVA's Notes from Peabody blog is closed by robots.txt (see `refused` in sources.json). Should Quad ask any of these
   for access, or is the corpus enough without them?
7. **Student-written pages on admissions sites.** One source (the Johns Hopkins "Hopkins Insider" post) is written by a
   current student and published by the admissions office. It is advice, not an essay; keep it?
   ([Johns Hopkins Admissions](https://apply.jhu.edu/hopkins-insider/application-resources-and-suggestions/))
8. **Purdue OWL's terms.** Purdue's pages say their material may not be reproduced without permission, under its fair
   use terms. The excerpts are short, cited, and used for an educational reader; the owner may want to confirm that
   this use is within those terms. ([Purdue OWL](https://owl.purdue.edu/owl/general_writing/punctuation/independent_and_dependent_clauses/runonsentences.html))
